Everyone should see this.

author: Calvin Kemph 🤠
review: There’s no guidebook for this sort of thing. There are situations where the act of filmmaking itself is deeply courageous. No Other Land is one such act of resilient bravery. Filmed over four years (from 2019 to 2023), the documentary captures the Israeli occupation of Masafer Yatta, a collection of hamlets along Palestine’s West Bank. The events of the story surround the expulsion of generations of families, as their homes and lifetimes of memories are bulldozed to make way for a training ground for military tanks.

You cannot act upon what you cannot see. And we are plagued by dead language and dead stories that serve people whose aim is nothing short of a dead world. And it is not enough to stand against these dissemblers. There has to be something in you, something that hungers for clarity. And you will need that hunger, because if you follow that path, soon enough you will find yourself confronting not just their myths, not just their stories, but your own.

author: preston
review: "Somebody watches something [e.g. a documentary on Palestine], they're touched... And then?" Not as overwhelming as expected - partly because even the repressive dynamic it shows is now superseded, coming from the days when Israel was 'just' an apartheid state - but its ultimate weakness is baked into the mix, like the poignant pointlessness of Basel constantly filming the abuse (hoping his images "might force the US to pressure Israel" lol) or hopefully checking the views on his latest social-media post. A village (and a nation) engaged in Sisyphean struggle, rebuilding their homes only to have them torn down again, veering between occasional optimism - the line about a single drop of water being insufficient but many drops of water eventually succeeding - and deep depression, finally focused on refusing to abandon the land because their only weapon is to stay (and because they have... well, check the title). Not so much indignant propaganda as a film about impotence, which is why it speaks so strongly to the current moment; the broader theme is trying to figure out how to effect change in the (post-)modern world, how to find new ways of shifting those in power when the old ways (protests, shaming) no longer work and the system operates as a well-oiled machine - the Israelis' actions are unfair but entirely legal, sanctioned by an Israeli court; then they slide into illegality, with attacks by the settlers, but by then the dynamic has been normalized - the Palestinian tragedy representative of a larger helplessness. But of course it's also about that tragedy, unfolding as inexorably as a slow-motion car crash - and it's also about the people, the kids forever resilient ("Are we going to live in a cave now?"), the friendship between two young men from opposite camps. Quietly heartbreaking.

author: Elyes
review: There's an external element to this film (and perhaps an internal one too) which is rather complicated and thorny. Saeed Taji Farouky has a pretty insightful twitter thread which delves into this. It's just one perspective on the film, but it's worth considering in light of its reception and how it may be discussed in western circles as it continues to garner more attention. Do I think this issue detracts significantly from the film? No of course not. It's still a very moving and harrowing look at real-time invasion—both militarily and by colonial settler civilians—of Israel on Palestinian homes and land in the West Bank. I'm particularly struck by the language dynamics here between both sides, it's something I had not noticed as strongly in other Palestinian films. Do I think it's not possible for an Israeli to collaborate fully with a Palestinian, be it in terms of making a film or overall political activism and support? No of course not. One of the best films of this century (Route 181) is co-directed by Michel Khleifi and Eyal Sivan. But I do think it bears food for thought to consider the balance of perspective and what gets illuminated when these kinds of collaborations occur.

author: Sam Rosenberg
review: Urgent and gutting documentary that demonstrates both the power and limits of documentation. Whether or not this will receive distribution (which I hope it will) and reach and affect the right people (which I fear it won’t) makes the final conversation between Basel and Yuval all the more haunting and poignant. “Someone watches something, they’re touched, and then what?”

author: jrhovind
review: “Somebody watches something, they’re touched, and then?” As invaluable and outraging as it is as an on-the-ground, present-moment account of the crimes of Zionist occupation, it’s a film that’s also exhaustedly, mercilessly self-aware about its own ultimate uselessness. “I don’t want this to happen,” Abraham, the Israeli humanitarian, wails at one point to one of the men whose lives have been reduced to an endless cycle of destruction and rebuilding, a man who can only respond, “But how will that help me?” If the behavior we see ample evidence of – not just from the soldiers and their animal cruelty, but from the talking heads on Israeli news, and the widespread social attitudes that make it all possible – offers little optimism that anything is going to ever change until there’s nothing left, then the bravery with which Basel turns his own camera on them becomes at once both defiant last stand and self-conscious chronicle of hopelessness. “Yes, but sometimes I think about it all, and I feel this huge depression in me.”

author: Poopie
review: To compare this documentary to others tackling the genocide that has been happening in Palestine for so long would be kind of pointless, considering that this is only getting the attention it deserves because of the recent events going on in Palestine that led to this documentary being made. Without the current events of the last year and a half, nowhere near as many people would be acknowledging an issue so huge and actively talking about and protesting against it, so it's overall a miracle that this documentary was made and even more so that it won best documentary at the academy awards. review: this film contains extremely important, frequently terrifying footage of the israeli dispossession and cleansing of a palestinian village via relentless and concerted campaigns of military and settler vigilante force, from arrests to stun grenades to bulldozers to disabling and lethal gun violence, documented and disseminated by film co-directors basel adra, a palestinian activist, and yuval abraham, an israeli journalist, between whom there is a sincere but uneasy friendship, underlined by the many inequalities of their experience of the land on either side of israeli apartheid. the silences and tensions constitute a fascinating aspect of the film, which often seems unsure of its usefulness, rubbing up against its own limits, because the representation and revelation of the coloniser’s crimes does not stem them (or perhaps it does, temporarily; an anecdote about tony blair visiting masafer yatta may ambiguously suggest that the strategy is waiting on the recognition and benevolence of western imperial governments— reinforcing an earlier hope expressed in the film that what it documents will induce the u.s. to pressure israel to suspend the demolition campaigns— the chances of which look increasingly remote). so how do we gain the power to do so? i was most unsure going into this what the role of yuval would be; i like that his presence and intentions as a “human rights israeli” are interrogated, though it is frustrating when a debate scene between yuval and one of the villagers seems to end prematurely, before the contradictions of his being a settler, the meaning of ending occupation, some vital political questions generated about the existence of israel, are really teased out. but sometimes its silences, and the film’s delicate reliance on images, are so powerful— like the lingering shot on harun abu aram’s mother after her interview with foreign journalists, the use of which already seems hopeless, slowly collapsing into tears. the film’s zeroing in on these individuals show how occupation has devastated their lives. basel talking about his uncertainty about having a family with no stability in the land is heartbreaking.

author: Paul Elliott
review: No Other Land, a documentary by a collective of Palestinian and Israeli filmmakers, stands as a powerful testament to resilience and solidarity amidst adversity. This film delves into the heart of the West Bank's Masafer Yatta, capturing the stark reality of occupation and the indomitable spirit of its people. It’s a documentary that challenges conventional filmmaking norms, with its very existence threatened during production, yet it emerges as an unflinching portrayal of a community's struggle for survival and justice. The film, which garnered accolades such as Best Documentary at the Berlin Film Festival, weaves together the narratives of Palestinian filmmaker Basel Adra, Israeli journalist Yuval Abraham, Palestinian farmer Hamdan Ballal, and Israeli cinematographer Rachel Szor. Their collective effort is a raw, unsensationalised depiction of life under occupation, as seen through the lens of those living it. Adra's footage, begun at the age of 15, serves as the backbone of the film, providing a deeply personal and poignant perspective.

author: Mathias
review: Attuned to the possibilities and limitations of the image as a tool of resistance. Basel, the central Palestinian activist and filmmaker, constantly confronts IDF troops, Israeli police, and Israeli settlers with the refrain, "I'm filming you, I'm filming you" - which is to say, the Israelis either know that what they are doing is wrong, or that they know that the rest of the world will never be convinced that what they are doing is right, and so cannot allow these images and footage of their actions to be displayed. Basel's "I'm filming you" is roughly equivalent to "I'm damning you and you know you deserve it." The action of filming, of the image, is also radicalized since the genocide in Gaza, with IDF soldiers being charged while abroad with war crimes due to what they have posted on social media. To see is to know. But is to know enough? The image is an act of resistance, but can the image alone achieve liberation? Basel wrestles with this throughout, constantly on his phone uploading footage and pictures and concerned with how many people have viewed his posts. Many Palestinians comment in the documentary on whether journalism has any efficacy for them anymore - what does it matter if no one cares? I think here on Mary Turfah's review in the Mubi Notebook, which criticizes the documentary for not grappling with the issue of armed resistance and October 7th. But I think that elides Basel's commitment. If one does not choose to take up the gun, how can one resist? You can take up the camera. Maybe knowing is not enough, but to not know never will be

author: TheMisfitPond
review: No Other Land is the single most important, powerful and soul crushing documentary to come out during my lifetime and a MUST SEE for any and everybody; especially every taxpayer whose dollars are funding this atrocity. As someone who has been paying attention to the ethnic cleansing and genocide of the Palestinian people for nearly a decade now, this documentary exposes the inhumane displacement of the Palestinian people and the destruction of their infrastructure (homes, land, water, power, schools, etc..) by the hands of the Israeli State, military and citizens (settlers) in the most gut-wrenching clear-cut way possible. What we see throughout the film through the eyes of Palestinian citizen Basel along with collaborative Israeli journalist Yuval, leaves no room for interpretation that Israel is occupying Palestinian land and accomplishing their establishment of an apartheid state through barbaric and soulless uses of violence. The amount of restraint and patience the Palestinians show in this film despite the every day nightmare they’re forced to wake up to is unprecedented. Every day is a day filled with desperation, violence and hopelessness; Yet, the tenacity to stay and attempt to rebuild what is repeatedly and expansively being destroyed and occupied is a divine strength like no other. No matter where you land on the political spectrum, this film will make you understand on a human level that nobody deserves to live without freedom, dignity and a place they can call home. So far, No Other Land has no official distribution in the United States for the obvious reason of our governmental, financial and political support for anything the State of Israel wants to do. There is a very limited theatrical distribution thanks to independent avenues making it temporarily available. If you live in the state of Georgia, it’s playing at the Tara Theatre. Please go and watch it while you can. Really hoping this wins Best Documentary at the Oscars. Maybe some kind of change will actually be possible…

author: cgavin
review: In a film which clocks in just over 90 minutes and covers several years in Masafer Yatta as its people reckon with brutal occupation, there is an unexpected attention paid to silence and distance. In the tangible tension between Basel and Yuval, there exists the lingering spectre of settler colonialism and cyclical bloodshed, regardless of the nobility of the latter’s intentions or the authenticity of their friendship. In the frequent shots of Basel on his phone, witnessing the reactions of the world, as bulldozers rumble and gunshots echo ceaselessly, it is a documentary that wrestles with the limitations of documentation. In the fleeting glimpses of Western politicians and journalists, there is a deafening confrontation with the uselessness of guilt or sorrow as ends in themselves; the need to rise above discourse and dopamine. There’s no disentangling yourself from this in a country that supports and funds the oppressors; there was an ad for McDonalds before the film, and another recruiting for the marines.

author: Nathan Spencer
review: The cinematic equivalent of a bullet fired point blank into your chest, something militant and masked Israeli settlers do to unarmed Palestinians (while IDF soldiers watch with glee) in No Other Land. The reason that this Oscar-winning Documentary still has no distribution is obvious: no one can see this film and walk away from it believing that Israel has ANY justification for the genocide they're inflicting on Palestinians, and people in power don't want a mass awakening to happen. In No Other Land, IDF soldiers roll up to schools that are in session, full of kids, and demolish them. They bulldoze homes with families inside, scrambling to remove belongings. They fill in wells and gardens with cement because a new law was signed making them illegal, even though they weren't the week before. They tell Palestinians that they must have a permit to rebuild their homes, but then deny every permit application. When the families rebuild anyway, IDF ghouls retaliate with more violence to suppress "illegal activities." Palestinians are not human beings in the eyes of war criminal Benjamin Netanyahu, and sadly, his decades-long propaganda machine has successfully brainwashed much of his country and the world into believing Israel is under siege by the people depicted in this film. Until October 7th, 2023, I knew next to nothing about this conflict other than that it had been happening for a long time. If asked, I'd have told you I supported Israel's efforts because that's what I'd been told was "right" my entire life. Since that moment, I've taken the time to read, listen, and learn the truth about what is still transpiring. A wide release for No Other Land is vital in stopping the genocide. But Hollywood is too cowardly to do so.

review: I have no quibbles with the descriptive markers lavished upon this film, be it "important" or "harrowing" or "devastating" - all of those are true and then some, because the footage depicted will and should shake you to your core. But I do think we're slightly reticent to critique the actual filmmaking here, which is a tad conventional and dry, footage without narrative, whose main "hook" per se (a tenuous friendship between the Palestinian and Israeli filmmakers) isn't fully probed and even occasionally feels artificially constructed. I think Basel's perspective and account is fully valuable, fascinating, and enriching on its own, so if you're going to introduce this dynamic, it needs to be purposeful and frankly more indicting, with takeaways beyond the observation that their conversations are awkward.

author: Josh Larsen
review: In spite of the clinical approach the filmmakers bring to No Other Land, the activist documentary nevertheless enrages. It boggles the mind (and moral compass) to watch ludicrously overarmed Israeli forces repeatedly destroy the homes, schools, and water-supply systems of Palestinian families who have lived on the land in question since before the establishment of the state of Israel. Aside from the video documentation of the demolitions—which includes, at one point, a soldier shooting an unarmed man over a struggle to keep his family’s generator—we get vignettes of everyday life for the villagers, in which quotidian observations carry an element of unspoken anguish. While being driven to school, a smiling girl looks out the window and starts a playful chant that doubles as a cry for dignity: “We have grass — it exists! We have a mountain — it exists! We have a chicken house – it exists! We have a house — it exists!” No Other Land exists to document that she knows what she’s talking about.

It's made by two friends, one Palestinian and one Israeli. We are reminded the latter come and go where he pleases. He has a home to go home to, while his friend has to live in a cave. Since I watched this the same evening as homes were burning in Los Angeles, (rightly or wrongly) I couldn't help but to compare the two. Tragic as the fires of California are, the homes aren't being systematically destroyed by fellow human beings. Watching as the Israeli military heartlessly plow through homes as if they're trash is infuriating. Even more painful is seeing the people who live in these homes watching their destruction.

author: Brian Formo
review: Devastating, intimate, and a necessary watch for anyone with a heartbeat. Decades of handheld camerawork documenting the occupation of the West Bank of Palestine, centering primarily on the forced evictions and demolishment of homes, schools, and water wells by the Israeli Army. The film includes footage of Basel's father leading protests against the army occupation as a twentysomething and also Basel leading protests at the same age as his father. A sympathetic Israeli journalist, Yuval, adds to the documentation of the heartless destruction of property. The years covered, 2019-2023, cement what the world is seeing now, that the complete eradication of the Palestinian population is the goal; now it just has a reaction to an attack to speed up the government's desires. The conclusion of the film, added after they finished the initial edit in Winter 2023, lays this bare. Settlers coming with guns, not just the military. Water lines cut off.

author: claira curtis
review: There’s this perpetual question presented here of whether documentation will bring relief for the Palestinian people under Israeli occupation. The lack of a definitive answer is devastating to take in, perhaps even more so now as we’ve seen the impact that thorough documentation of an ongoing genocide has had on US politicians (next to none). Thankful for Basel Adra’s dedication to shedding light on the horrific actions of Israel against his people despite how directly it puts his life in danger and his well being at risk, but I am also filled with an unending sense of rage that he has had to do so in the first place and for such a prolonged part of his life. Adra was documenting further attacks by armed settlers on Masafer Yatta as recently as February 3rd, 2025. 5 days ago. A ceasefire is not enough (nor was it ever going to be enough). Israel continues in its seemingly never-ending desire to eradicate the Palestinian people. I have to hope that No Other Land is playing a part in ensuring they do not succeed. The world sees what Israel is doing more and more with each passing day. Palestine will be free.

author: Taylor Williams
review: A movie about witnessing genocide firsthand as directly as we possibly can from our position of comfort, but also a movie reckoning with its own usefulness. Basel calls Yuval out for his optimism that a few articles gaining traction will put a stop to apartheid, and in many ways the film itself is an extension of the journalistic endeavors it documents. It is already wary of the hearts and minds it is being shown to, the divide between the people who will watch this movie that don’t actually need it to motivate their support for Palestine (though witnessing as unflinchingly as we do here is necessary to avoid desensitization), and the people who will watch and refuse to change their perspective despite the persecution shown in empirical bluntness. The fact that its own Letterboxd page was briefly vandalized to describe it as terrorist propoganda is testament enough to the strength of the Zionist wool pulled over this latter group’s eyes, and I think the film does a good job staying self-aware wrt its activist potential.

A story about a boy with Down syndrome being eaten alive by IDF soldier's dog and calling the dog ‘honey stop’ because he doesn't know what's happening—only for his family to return and find his body ripped apart. A story about a little boy wandering the ruins alone because he has no one left in this world waiting for his turn to come. A story of a father mourning his barely alive baby, the child’s bones show through the thin skin, a victim of severe malnutrition. But there is nothing the father can do—Israel has cut off all food supplies to Gaza. A story of a man calmly collecting the scattered body parts of his children, placing them in a bag, and walking away. A story of a boy carrying a bloodied backpack and saying, 'This is my brother I carry with me.’ I just can't write no more, my eyes are full of tears right now, but if I try to tell all the stories I'll never finish writing. author: Josh Larsen
review: Even as my understanding of Fremen and Harkonnens and Bene Gesserit becomes increasingly confused—to say nothing of trying to keep track of the mounting pile of names for Paul Atreides (Timothee Chalamet)—the spell cast by Dune and now Dune: Part Two continues to hold me enthralled. Must be the spice. You’ll have to look for a spirited defense of the movie’s snowballing narrative, as well as the complicated character motivations driving it, elsewhere. I’m here to tell you to set much of that aside, breathe in the precious spice that has brought warring parties to the desert planet of Arrakis, and simply take the trip. It’s not Paul and his perplexing quest to lead the indigenous Fremen in a defense of their world that captivates me about Dune: Part Two. Instead, it’s the sounds of whirring machines in vast, hollow spaces; the textures of the fabrics and armor worn by the massive cast of characters; and the ever-shifting, sifting play of sand and light on a planet that seems to exist of only those two things. (In some ways cinematographer Greig Fraser is as much the auteur of this series as director Denis Villeneuve.) Like its predecessor, Dune: Part Two gets in your nostrils, employing the sensuousness of cinema to put you—bodily—in a wholly original time and place. Beyond that sand, Part Two also incisively incorporates the unexpected element of water, presented here as precious, even holy. As a religious narrative, Part Two is a bit unsteady—at turns provocative and diffuse—but its use of water is wholly engrossing. Sucked from the corpses of slain enemies so that others might live or preserved from the bodies of lost compatriots to be added to a sacred well, water in Dune: Part Two has both an intriguing spiritual import and an earthly materiality. Beneath those dusty nostrils, you can feel it on your lips. (With Zendaya, given more to do this time but largely stuck in a perfunctory romance; Javier Bardem, adding gravitas but also, on occasion, a blessedly light touch; and Austin Butler, channeling all his Elvis charisma into a new villain, essentially a nightclub Nosferatu who’s picky about his knives.)

author: Brian Tallerico
review: The word that will likely be used most often to describe Denis Villeneuve’s “Dune: Part Two” is “massive.” Expect a whole lot of variations on the words “epic” and “spectacle” too. Whatever big words you apply to the result, Villeneuve undeniably did not approach Frank Herbert’s beloved sci-fi novel with modest aspirations, and it’s his ambition, along with the top tier of behind-the-scenes craftspeople with whom he collaborated, that have paid off in this superior follow-up to the Oscar-winning 2021 film. While that beloved blockbuster often felt like half a film, “Dune: Part Two” locates significantly higher stakes on Arrakis, while injecting just enough humor and nuanced themes about power and fanaticism to flavor the old-fashioned storytelling. More than a simple savior or chosen one story, “Dune: Part Two” is a robust piece of filmmaking, a reminder that this kind of broad-scale blockbuster can be done with artistry and flair.

review: I can’t believe this is what constitutes contemporary epic filmmaking. I have a general issue with Denis Villeneuve’s visual approach to these films that begin with the first “Dune.” It’s all so self-serious, so drab and lacking any vitality. I have to squint at the screen to tell which shade of beige is any given character. It doesn’t help that I also find Timothée Chalamet and Zendaya equally forgettable. Every note they hit feels false. To a point, that is, of course intended. These are two young warriors who are projecting more than they are internalizing. And yet, when someone like Austin Butler pops up, someone who is aware of how silly this all is and is willing to at least play with that tone—even if his attempts are swallowed whole by the overbaked surroundings—both Chalamet and Zendaya are revealed to be distinctly underwhelming.

author: Josh Lewis
review: With all the effective medieval political intrigue and Greek tragedy table-setting of the first movie out of the way, Denis is free to make the muscular, military space opera Lawrence of Arabia meets The Last Temptation of Christ he was clearly itching to make—where Paul is both a naïve crazy ass white boy who falls in love with/learns the ways of the desert and becomes a guerilla revolutionary fighter against his own oppressive political class, but also a tortured messiah figure who has visions of a painful, inevitable destiny he learns to stop doubting/resisting and accept. The key to Herbert’s eco-horror, anti-imperialist fable that Villeneuve rightfully hones in on is that all the sympathy garnered by briefly experiencing what it might feel like to be the victim of a merciless political trap is weaponized into getting you swept up in the momentum of righteous revenge against those who orchestrated it (namely the grotesque Baron and his gluttonous, brutal quest for power) and furthermore desire to see everyone equally if not even moreso under their cruel rule (the Fremen) cathartically liberated from it. But the precise method available to Paul in order to seize this control and vengefully right this wrong is a double-edged sword that involves the crafting and manipulation of religious myth and fervor as a violent political tool that has rippling consequences and leads to uncontrollable horrors. Coming soon to an IMAX screen near you!

author: alexcolemann
review: This is why we fucking make movies. I’m grateful I was able to stay alive long enough to witness this masterpiece. Masterpiece somehow being an understatement, this is a project that shouldn’t be possible but Denis and the crew — with their God given talents — made dreams come true. It’s a truly grand experience and maybe the greatest thing I’ve ever seen. The performances (Timmy, Rebecca, Zendaya, Austin and Javier Bardem specifically) are all worthy of Oscar praise and moved me to my core. review: “Spider-Man: Across the Spider-Verse” explodes onto screens this week, building on the foundation of the masterful “Spider-Man: Into the Spider-Verse” with stunning animation, unforgettable characters, and complex themes. The first note I took after seeing it was “so much movie.” Like the work of a young artist who refuses to be restrained by the borders of the frame, “Across the Spider-Verse” is loaded with incredible imagery and fascinating ideas. It is a smart, thrilling piece of work that reminded me of other great part twos like “The Dark Knight” and “The Empire Strikes Back.” Like those films, it leaves viewers anxiously anticipating the next chapter (which will come in March 2024), and it earns its cliffhangers by grounding them in a story of young people refusing to submit to a concept of what a hero’s arc needs to be.

author: AdamAB
review: I would love to go against the grain and say Across the Spider-Verse is an overly hyped symbol of mediocrity. However, I was completely hypnotised by the incredible amount of detail in each painstakingly designed frame. The varying worlds are visually distinct, and this isn’t a case of beautiful but stilted imagery; this is a wildly kinetic and propulsive cinematic experience. It is certainly a more unwieldy beast than its predecessor, a common feature for a sequel, and its lack of finality may prove grating to some. Still, this feels like a significant landmark in animation and in the wider superhero genre as a whole.

author: Adam Nayman
review: The subject of this series is genuinely vital and contemporary: it’s about occupying, renovating and subdividing intellectual property. Sony and Marvel’s biter corporate compromise has yielded two enjoyably self-aware films that simultaneously satirize and celebrate the ready abundance of Spider-Man related content; this one pivots on the possibility that messing with the canon is not only possible but liberating. Deep pocketed technical mastery yoked to exuberant, expressive conceptual impulses - plus more good visual, verbal, and contextual jokes than strictly necessary - equals a very good time at the movies, and the cliffhanger is fine by me, not least of all because the film is already too long as it is.

author: Matt Singer
review: There are generally two types of sequels: The ones that rehash the previous film’s success for financial gain, and the ones that use the previous film’s success as a license to experiment. Spider-Man: Across the Spider-Verse isn’t just that second kind of sequel, it’s actually about making precisely that sort of movie. Its real villain isn’t the Vulture or the Spot, it’s storytelling orthodoxy; the idea that you must create a work of art in a certain way simply because that’s how it’s always been done.

author: Sethsreviews
review: It’s extremely rare that a sequel will manage to meet the levels of its monumental predecessor, but Spider-Man: Across the Spider-Verse manages to accomplish just that. The artistry is second to none, a visual feast that doesn’t pull any punches when it comes to providing jaw-dropping sequences. Multi-verse story telling at its finest, and even when it does lose a sense of direction, it manages to pull itself back in and regain focus. Dare I say it, one of Marvel’s best projects to date (alongside the first).

author: Edward
review: Not many movies contest with the emotional level that’s seen in How To Make Millions before Grandma Dies. An 126 minute rollercoaster - as we witness M’s metamorphosis into a conscious appreciator of the presence. It hooks onto us. We reflect on our lives and ask the question - did we waste it? I think what makes the movie is great is the contrast between M and Amah. They way they go through life, and what they enjoy, is so powerfully different. Yet as they come closer to one another, they realise the only thing they can truly appreciate - is now. The movie touches to everyone. As we grow up, our gap of independence inevitably widens. And we sadly forget to spend time with those who were always with us, from birth to death. The film is just magical, it really connected with me as I constantly asked myself of how valuably I have spent my time. Thank you to another Asian grandparent for making me really sad.

review: I can see this film shares so many relatabilities to many Indonesian people, as evidence by the majority of the reviews here. Thailand and Indonesia markedly share numerous cultural similarities, particularly concerning the veneration of elders, traditional familial roles, and the pervasive superstitions that permeate life and death. The film’s portrayal of a modest lifestyle, close-knit familial bonds, and the prioritization of spiritual merit over material opulence strikes a familiar and authentic chord with Indonesian viewers. The depiction of food, family gatherings, and quotidian dialogues also serves to create an immediate and compelling sense of cultural alignment too.

author: ornithopter
review: Entertaining and funny enough. But I suspect after a few months of discourse many will find this really does not have much going on. It's idiosyncratic, it is a unique object in American popular cinema, in terms of its content. But the structure is wholly conventional and the entire film is delivered as one clean straight line. I was not left with any lingering discomfort or contradiction. Sometimes for better but mostly for worse, PTA is a filmmaker who works almost entirely from intuition. And at the end of the day, when imagination fails, he reaches for 'quality filmmaking.' I respect his tendency to challenge himself by periodically resetting his plot's milieu, but at no point do I feel he would truly upset things by giving up his style. The film is in fact an incredibly expensive exercise in making something mannered and picked over seem hardscrabble and grungy. Much like a period film, verisimilitude is the goal. 'What an excellent job this film does of evoking the present!' But that's the problem. It's an evocation of signifiers with no risk or skin in the game. It will receive praise because it is the apotheosis of both our lackluster film culture and political discourse. It is an excellent, understandable, enjoyable fill-in for radicalism.

review: The same way Get Out turned out to perfectly anticipate the Zeitgeist of the first Trump era, here we have a film that presciently nails the vibe of the deranged sequel. It's there in the aesthetics, of course: migrants in zip-ties, APCs in civilian streets. But also, in his strange mock-Pynchonian way, PTA nails what it feels like to live through the second Trump era. The sense of a government run according to the sexual whims of leathery, oddly-jacked old men. An oligarchy whose utter ridiculousness does not erase the fact that their ideology is largely indistinguishable from Nazis'. A regime that has essentially declared war on its own citizens. What else is there to do but laugh, and resist any way you can?

author: Brian Tallerico
review: Aren’t you tired of fighting? Paul Thomas Anderson’s “One Battle After Another” comes along at a time in world history in which conflict seems to be the daily duty, turning Thomas Pynchon’s ’80s-set Vineland into a deeply humanist story of rebellion that will be read as 2020s political commentary despite never using terms like MAGA or Antifa. Anderson’s phenomenal screenplay is a timeless story of resistance, one that playfully weaves together influences as broad-reaching as the true story of Weather Underground and cinematic depictions of rebellion, but it’s also a remarkably propulsive, fun, and eventually moving piece of work about the human beings caught up in the chaotic machine. It’s a live wire that drops in the first scene, setting off sparks for the next 162 minutes.

author: Dok
review: For years now, the main mode of online film discourse has been about whether or not various blockbusters are subtextually woke (good) or subtextually unwoke (bad), so it's funny and refreshing that the first deliberately woke studio product takes pains to quote "The Revolution Will Not Be Televised" multiple times. Moving the skeleton of Vineland to the present day demystifies the cliche of the sixties as a magical time where The One Revolution *almost* happened in favor of a more applicable portrayal of left-wing action both eternally ongoing and stymied by its practitioners being betrayed, compromised, or just plain getting old. This is the first work of art I know of that engages with the weird way all political corners have fetishized the Black Woman Revolutionary, breaking complex and fallible human beings on the wheel once they're no longer comfortably sexy Pam Grier action figures (most reviews I've seen so far also engage in this, in the same way that most of the first reactions to Do the Right Thing were about whether or not windows are good). Even fascism's kind of lost its mojo: it's certainly on top, but Pynchon's invincible supercop holds no dark, transgressive allure now that nationalist rallies air on cable tv set to the music of Cats. Like most honest art, this is largely about failure, but it also finds the hope lost for adventurism in community and generational renewal, there are no definitive victories but sturdier preparations for...well, see the title.

author: Filipe Furtado
review: A very good strengthening of a fracture family movie and sometimes exciting chase picture in the middle of a lot of bloat. Anderson can be a very uneven filmmaker, and he is not one to turn an idea down, something that can be good and bad. He is a firm believer that a well placed joke can cover a lot of sins, and he goes to this well a lot on this with mixed results, but I do like that a certain strand of elitist cinephile ideal filmmaker does have these instincts. One Battle After Another will get discussed mostly in terms of its politics because we live in a literalist time, and people see signposts and go wild on them. On those terms, this is a very mixed bag and at times outright exploitative without having much to say. The scenes with Del Toro (who is playing the more successful of the movie's many father figures) running things while his city falls into military takeover chaos do have some force, but most of the scenes suggesting camps and military/revolutionary action are muddled. Anderson has always been interested in sociological observation, one of the reasons he has concentrated on historical pieces, but he usually isn't very comfortable with political discourse. There Will Be Blood has many interesting things on the formation of American capital and the men behind it while trying as much as possible to ignore its original author's politics, and by the same token, he milks Pynchon's counterculture hangover for a certain imaginary while struggling with its meaning beyond a vague idea about how its scenario is supposedly to remain relevant. The movie works better in this vein as a phantasmagoria of current American paranoia, and keeping with its many doublings, one that nods towards left and right fantasies about each other. The French 75 is very close to what strands of the American right imagine "Antifa" to be (right down to its prominence of Black women) than any sort of past/present suggestion, although the cabal Penn wants to join is simultaneously creepy/funny and past the sell date, but they clearly intend to mirror each other. As for actual politics, Anderson can’t do much more than general platitudes and 70s needle drops. There is also a lot on libido and sexual hangups as fuel to all this, something that Anderson has hinted at in the past as well, and it is all suggestive but a little underdeveloped. It is a very straightforward movie, with different groups chasing each other that keeps adding busy bits of business and then works itself out of it by easy outs: a too-smooth interrogation, a small character change of heart, the competing organizations shadowy reach, a car getting hotwired. At some point, it does get a little exhausting, and the strings to make it seem larger than it really is show too much. The movie is exciting, and Anderson does show his pleasure at having all those fireworks Di Caprio patronage brings to him. In this it reminds me of Magnolia, a similar flex from early in his career that often gets by on the mix of the wunderkind energy and the shameless of it all even when the noise can feel questionable. One Battle After Another is a better movie because Anderson is a quarter of century later a much better filmmaker, but he seems far less in control than he was in his past few movies. (In a curious echo current Warner chair Michael De Luca was New Line head of production when Magnolia got made). The muscle is impressive, and those large-scale scenes do have at least some power. The big action finale is very good, if a little oversold, but the freneticism works, and the road landscapes do have a presence that stays in the mind. It has resources that current good action movies lack and some ingenuity that most big-budget movies can't suggest. It is also too clever at times, full of twists and delays that are supposed to highlight Anderson's auteurial touch that are arguably less effective than a more meat-and-potatoes approach. Everything is set around mirrors and doubles, with DiCaprio and Penn chasing after their daughter, past and present action echoing each other, multiple delusions and failures, and so on. The frantic opening plays into some of Anderson's dramatic weaknesses, but the movie improves a lot once it settles and can at least appreciate the idea of opening with what is really backstory (it's more or less the same thing Drive My Car does at a completely different pace and intentions). I'm not sure about how heightened Penn's scenes and performance are pitched, but Anderson's do wonders at setting them against DiCaprio's mellower scenes. The movie's shift between them is often its most impressive achievement. It is played at the cartoonish idea many have of Pynchon, but this shift allowed it to keep its emotional stakes, more personal than political, resonant. One Battle After Another is at its best in DiCaprio's desperate desire to find Infiniti. They barely share scenes, but his need does give the movie a good focus. DiCaprio is quite wonderful throughout, very funny in his fuckup pothead routine, but consistently moving. He's talking about not being able to do her hair; it might be the most I ever liked DiCaprio in anything. Failed authority figures used to be a strong part of Anderson's work that has been less present in the last decade or so, and this differs from his early work in actually liking the dad despite his inefficiency (it should be pointed out that DiCaprio doesn't really do much through this) and being mostly from his perspective. DiCaprio's scenes with Del Toro are especially great; both actors respond to each other so well, and Anderson's finds keep the pace frantic while the two men relaxed around each other set a smoother tone. If everything else were as good as those scenes, this would be as great as its large praise suggests. Most of it is a victim of the background noise, but it is easy to admire even when it's tripping on itself.

review: Completely fucking mad. The real deal. A wonderful father/daughter espionage thriller, kind of THE generation-defining blockbuster. This will be looked back on as miles ahead of its years in decades to come. Defies all cinematic logic in that it barely takes a single breath yet never feels like there is too much going on - like being continuously punched in the face but still craving more. Miracle how this works as well as it does! Full of energy. dominated by entirely opposite extremes of the spectrum, pulling for long-past periods. Sean Penn is wickedly evil, and there aren't many DiCaprio performances I would choose over this one. Seriously though, Sean Penn is unbelievable. I'm still on edge an hour after watching. Inject it! The best of the year! Cloud nine.
